Short answers to the questions that come up most, with links to the guide that
covers each topic in depth.

## Getting started

### What do I need before I can use staRburst?

- An AWS account, with credentials available to R (see
  [credentials](#which-aws-credentials-does-it-use) below).
- **Docker running on your machine.** staRburst builds the worker image locally
  with `docker buildx` and pushes it to your ECR repository. You only pay this
  build once per environment (see [the first run](#why-is-my-first-run-so-slow)).
- A one-time `starburst_setup()`, which creates the S3 bucket, ECR repository,
  ECS cluster, IAM roles, and the default EC2 capacity provider.

The [Getting Started](getting-started.html) guide walks through all three.

### Which function should I use?

Start with `starburst_map()`. If you already have `future`, `future.apply`, or
`furrr` code, set `plan(starburst)` and leave the rest unchanged. Use
`starburst_session()` for long jobs you want to close R and come back to. The
[comparison table](getting-started.html#which-api-should-i-use) has the
full list.

### EC2 or Fargate?

EC2 is the default and the right choice for most work. It's cheaper with Spot
(also the default), lets you pick any instance type, and supports warm pools.
Fargate (`launch_type = "FARGATE"`) is a serverless option that needs no
capacity provider, but it has cold-start latency and is limited by your
account's Fargate vCPU quota. See
[Which backend?](getting-started.html#which-backend-ec2-default-vs-fargate).

### Does it work with `furrr`, `future.apply`, and `targets`?

Yes. Anything built on `future` runs on staRburst once `plan(starburst, ...)` is
active:

```{r}
library(furrr)
plan(starburst, workers = 50)
results <- future_map(inputs, slow_function)
```

## Environment and data

### Why is my first run so slow?

The first run builds a Docker image containing your R packages. That takes
roughly 5–10 minutes. The image is tagged with a hash of your `renv.lock` and
cached in ECR, so later runs with the same lockfile reuse it. Changing your
lockfile, for example by installing or upgrading a package and snapshotting,
triggers a rebuild.

Worker startup itself (launching instances and pulling the image) adds about
90 seconds per cold run. Running many jobs against one warm cluster spreads
that cost out; see the [Performance](performance.html) guide.

### Which R packages are available on the workers?

The packages in your project's `renv.lock`. If no lockfile is found, staRburst
creates one with `renv::snapshot()`. To change what the workers have, update
your lockfile. The next run detects the new hash and rebuilds the image.

### My R version has no public base image. What happens?

Public base images are published only for specific R releases (currently
4.5.3 and 4.6.1). On any other R version, staRburst builds a private base image
in your ECR instead, a one-time 3–5 minute step per R version. Use
staRburst 0.3.10 or later: earlier versions' base-image template could silently
produce images without `qs2`, and workers built from them fail to read their
tasks.

### What gets uploaded? Is my whole workspace sent?

No. For each task, staRburst uploads the function, that task's input, and the
globals the function actually references. Large datasets should go to S3 once,
and each worker reads them from there. See
[Working with Data](getting-started.html#working-with-data) and the
"don't serialize huge objects to every worker" pitfall in the
[Performance](performance.html) guide.

## Cost

### How much will a job cost?

Estimate before you run. `starburst_estimate()` times a small sample of your
tasks locally and projects the cloud time and cost:

```{r}
starburst_estimate(inputs, slow_function, workers = 50)
```

You can also set a ceiling so that over-budget jobs refuse to start:

```{r}
starburst_config(max_hourly_cost = 10, cost_alert_threshold = 5)
```

Reported costs are **estimates**: measured runtime multiplied by the current AWS
price, looked up live and cached, with built-in rates as an offline fallback.
They are not AWS billing figures.

### What does staRburst cost when I'm not running anything?

Setup itself launches nothing billable. The EC2 capacity provider is created at
zero instances. What persists between jobs:

- **ECR images.** Storage for your worker images, typically cents to a dollar a
  month. Pass `ecr_image_ttl_days` to `starburst_setup()` to expire old images
  automatically, or run `starburst_cleanup_ecr()`.
- **S3 objects.** Job inputs and results are removed when a job finishes, unless
  you set `starburst_config(auto_cleanup_s3 = FALSE)`. Detached sessions keep
  their results in S3 until you call `session$cleanup(force = TRUE)`.
- **Detached-session workers.** These keep running until the session finishes,
  hits its `session_timeout` or `absolute_timeout`, or you call
  `session$cleanup()`.

To confirm nothing is still running, check `starburst_list_sessions()` and the
EC2 and ECS consoles. The [Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html) guide's
"High Costs / Runaway Workers" section shows how to find and stop leftovers.
Setting an AWS Budgets alert is also a good idea.

## Scale and limits

### How many workers can I use?

Up to 500 per plan. staRburst refuses larger requests to protect you from
accidental runaway costs. On EC2, your account's EC2 instance limits also apply.
On Fargate, your Fargate vCPU quota applies: staRburst runs the job in waves if
you ask for more than the quota allows, and `starburst_quota_status()` and
`starburst_request_quota_increase()` help you raise it.

### Why isn't my job faster on the cloud?

Usually because each task is too small. Every task pays fixed overhead
(serialization plus S3 round-trips), so thousands of sub-second tasks run slower
than they would locally. Batch them into fewer, larger tasks, and use no more
workers than you have tasks. The [Workload Shapes](workload-shapes.html)
guide covers this with measured numbers.

## Accounts and operations

### Which AWS credentials does it use?

Whatever the standard AWS credential chain finds, through the `paws` SDK:
environment variables, a named profile (`AWS_PROFILE`), AWS SSO profiles, or an
IAM role when running on EC2 or ECS. Credentials never go in your code or in S3.
The workers use their own IAM role. See [Security](security.html).

### Which region does it run in?

The region you passed to `starburst_setup()` (default `us-east-1`), stored in
your staRburst config. Most functions also take a `region` argument, but your
bucket, repository, and cluster live in the setup region.

### Can I close R while a job is running?

Yes, with a detached session:

```{r}
session <- starburst_session(workers = 20)
session$submit(quote(long_simulation()))
id <- session$session_id

# ...later, in a new R session:
session <- starburst_session_attach(id)
results <- session$collect(wait = TRUE)
```

See the [Detached Sessions](detached-sessions.html) guide.

### Where are the worker logs?

In CloudWatch Logs. Read them from R with `starburst_logs()`, or for a single
task with `starburst_logs(task_id = ...)`. The
[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.html) guide lists common error patterns
and what they mean.
